planting.note: Sow fresh seed in warm, humid conditions and transplant container-grown palms after frost danger has passed into rich, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; this species demands more warmth and moisture than the closely related king palm.

directions: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, siting this single-trunked feather palm where it has overhead clearance for its smooth gray-green crownshaft and gracefully arching fronds. Keep soil consistently moist and provide regular feeding with a palm-specific fertilizer, since this species is less drought-tolerant and slightly less cold-hardy than Archontophoenix cunninghamiana, the more commonly planted king palm. Showy sprays of lavender to white flowers emerge below the crownshaft and are followed by clusters of bright red fruit that attract birds. Best grown in frost-free tropical and near-tropical landscapes as a fast-growing specimen or avenue tree.

planting.note: Sow fresh seed in warm, well-drained medium and transplant young palms only after all frost danger has passed into sunny, sharply drained soil; growth is notoriously slow, especially in the juvenile years before the trunk begins forming its characteristic fiber coat.

directions: Site in full sun on sharply drained, sandy or rocky soil, giving this slow-growing Cuban endemic room to develop its signature dense shag of curling gray-white leaf fibers that cloak the entire trunk. Once established it is highly drought- and salt-tolerant, making it a prized specimen in xeric and coastal landscapes, though plants remain very slow to size up and are correspondingly expensive in the nursery trade. Small palmate fan leaves top the fiber-wrapped trunk, and inconspicuous flower clusters are followed by small purple-black fruit. Avoid overwatering and heavy soils, which encourage rot in this otherwise tough, long-lived palm.

planting.note: Sow fresh seed in warm, moist medium and transplant into deep, rich, well-drained soil in full sun once temperatures stay reliably warm; this is the tallest of the royal palms and needs ample overhead and root space from the start.

directions: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, allowing generous overhead clearance for this towering feather palm, which grows taller and with a more slender, uniformly columnar gray trunk than the more widely planted Cuban royal palm, Roystonea regia. The smooth green crownshaft and large arching fronds give the crown a formal, stately look well suited to grand avenue plantings in frost-free tropical regions. Provide consistent moisture and regular palm fertilizer during the establishment period, after which the species tolerates occasional flooding and a range of soils. Historically a signature tree of Caribbean island landscapes and botanical gardens.

planting.note: Sow fresh seed in warm, well-drained potting mix and keep indoors or transplant outdoors only after frost danger has passed in frost-free climates; this species is commonly braided and grown as a houseplant far more often than it is planted in the ground.

directions: Grow in bright, indirect light or partial outdoor shade in well-drained, humus-rich soil, allowing the soil to dry slightly between waterings since this swollen-trunked tree stores moisture and resents constantly soggy roots. Pachira glabra is frequently sold under the common name 'money tree' with its trunk braided while young, and it is readily distinguished from the similar Pachira aquatica by its creamy-white, non-showy flower petals rather than the larger, dramatic red-and-white blooms of that species. Glossy palmate leaves radiate from upright stems, and mature plants in warm climates produce woody pods containing edible, chestnut-like seeds. Indoors, rotate occasionally for even light and fertilize lightly during the growing season.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Sow seed in a warm nursery bed or containers and transplant young trees in spring into deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; this fast-growing species tolerates more warmth and humidity than its relative Toona sinensis.

directions: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, giving this fast-growing deciduous tree ample room for its broad, spreading crown and large pinnately compound leaves that flush coppery-red before maturing to green. Fragrant, creamy-white flower panicles appear in late spring and are followed by woody capsules that split to release winged seeds. Valued historically for its fine, mahogany-like timber and still widely planted as a shade or avenue tree in subtropical and warm-temperate regions, it grows considerably larger and faster than the closely related, vegetable-grown Toona sinensis. Prune to shape while young, as branches can be brittle in strong wind.

planting.note: Scarify or soak seed before sowing in warm, well-drained medium, and transplant into deep, fertile soil in full sun once temperatures stay reliably warm; growth to flowering and seed-bearing size takes many years.

directions: Site in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, allowing room for this slow-growing legume tree to develop its broad canopy of compound leaves with rounded leaflets. Clusters of small, fragrant lilac-white pea-like flowers appear in summer, followed by flat, papery seed pods typical of the genus. Long prized and now severely overharvested in the wild for its dense, richly figured heartwood used in fine furniture and musical instruments, it is CITES-listed and today is grown mainly in arboreta, conservation plantings, and warm-climate botanical collections rather than commercial timber stands. Provide consistent moisture while young; established trees tolerate brief dry spells.
